item.title: Product Engineering
item.description:
A new title has been popping in conversations that I’m not terribly familiar with: Product Engineering. Google trends shows that it started to really pop up January 2022.

It’s relatively new to me, so let’s see who’s written about it:

  • PostHog: https://posthog.com/product-engineer/what-is-a-product-engineer
    • They quote incident.io, which I can’t actually find the source
    • https://posthog.com/blog/why-product-engineering-is-so-fun
  • Shopify(2018): https://sherifmansour.medium.com/product-engineers-f424da766871
  • Lee Robison(https://leerob.com/product-engineers)
  • Pragmatic Engineer(2019): https://blog.pragmaticengineer.com/the-product-minded-engineer/#tips-to-become-a-more-product-minded-engineer

A lot went right, but a lot went wrong. In my opinion, the biggest mistake made was thinking rebranding some roles as DevOps engineers without changing the underlying culture. I write this to provide myself a framework that hopefully amplifies the lessons learned from DeVops practices, without going through the pain of having to explain a new job title/function/

item.title: Proving Value in the Agentic Era
item.description: A recent article came out from Uber where they burned through a years worth of budget in the first four months of the year. The associated hackernews thread on is quite worthwhile to read through. Agents, and agentic coding, has proven to be more divisive in 6 months than k8s has in almost a decade of it’s existence. Proponents of it think the value is self explanatory and requires no further proof. Nay sayers claim not only is the spend on tokens shameful, the resulting work requires 10x the time to clean up. Like most things, the truth is somewhere between the two. But there’s something really important that’s worthwhile considering: Could you prove today that agents have provided value in your day to day life?

item.title: Effective Agentic Coding
item.description:
I want to start capturing different ways of using agentic tools effectively. Most of the discourse I see online around agentic tools such as Claude/Codex/Gemini focus around how to generate code. However, my personal experience has been that writing code is likely the last thing I end up using the tooling for. After ~4 months of using agentic tools, I’ve started to recognize distinct workflows:

  1. research and investigate
  2. data gathering
  3. learn and experiment
  4. explore implementation details
  5. Finally, coding

Let me explain each of these areas in a detail.

item.title: gRPC
item.description: I’ve heard of gRPC for quite some time, ran many applications in my life as a platform engineer that had gRPC endpoints, but never directly contributed to it. gRPC is coming up more frequently now that I’m working as a backend engineer, and I feel like I need to dive deeper into the fundamentals. The code is intuitive enough to update existing handlers. But what happens if you need to create a new handler? Or if you need to update how the client is initialized?

item.title: Tyranny of Pencil and Paper
item.description: Windsurfer being aqcuired by OpenAI Cognition is making me reconsider the way I work. I have been skeptical that LLM’s will be the next major revolution in technology. Experience has provided enough context to have heard many other technologies claim they’ll usher in a new era of tech. There’s still this small pit of fear that I am wrong on this and miss out on a potentially career ending mistake.

item.title: Faro
item.description:
Disclaimer! I work at Grafana Labs and am writing this in my personal time to explore the product

I want to monitor traffic to this site and do it in a way that maintains privacy. In the past I’ve used Google Analytics, which I’m opting not to use due to the amount of data collected.

Here are some of the things I’d like to track:

  • How many users visited my website, broken down by page
  • How long does a user stay?
  • How much data is transmitted?
  • How well does the page perform?

Since I work at Grafana, I am biased towards using Grafana Faro.

item.title: Squarespace
item.description: I use squarespace for markpoko.dev’s DNS records, though not by choice. Up until 2024, I had used Google domains to handle my DNS thingy. At the time it made sense as I was diving deep into learning GCP. There was a nice integration between Cloud Run and Google Domains, making it trivial to expose services over a DNS entry. As Google does, the project was shut down and sold off to Squarespace.
